content:
The Australian government has appointed former Liberal minister Philip Ruddock to lead a review of whether current laws adequately protect the human right to religious freedom. Announced by cabinet on Wednesday, the review was initiated partly to preempt contentious debates over proposed religious amendments to the forthcoming same-sex marriage bill, following the national “Yes” vote in the postal survey.

***
While the review aims to provide clarity and reduce political tension, Treasurer Scott Morrison emphasized that it is “no substitute” for the legislative amendments sought by some conservatives. Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull underscored the timeliness of the review, noting the need for careful examination of religious freedom in the context of impending marriage equality legislation and the broader societal implications of the postal survey outcome.

***
There is internal division within the Liberal Party regarding the timing and scope of religious freedom legislation. Senior conservatives such as Peter Dutton and Mathias Cormann have indicated support for considering a standalone religious freedom bill next year, separate from the marriage legislation. In contrast, Morrison and Liberal senator David Fawcett maintain that any such measures should be addressed concurrently with the marriage bill to ensure coherence and avoid legislative fragmentation.

***
Ruddock has been tasked with delivering his findings by 31 March. His review will assess a range of proposals that have emerged recently — many of which extend well beyond marriage-related concerns — and evaluate their appropriateness, feasibility, and potential impacts. Turnbull cautioned that broad, loosely drafted protections risk creating legal uncertainty, particularly warning against “generally worded bill of rights-style declarations” that could lead to unintended consequences in practice.

***
Turnbull defended Ruddock’s appointment by highlighting his prior service as Australia’s special envoy for human rights, underscoring his expertise and credibility on matters of international and domestic human rights law. Describing the review as a “timely expert stocktake,” the Prime Minister stressed its role in informing future, evidence-based legislative reforms — rather than serving as a rushed political response — and reiterated the government’s commitment to balancing religious freedom with other fundamental rights.
